title: What Makes a Must-Have Christmas Toy?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore what makes a toy a "must-have" Christmas toy. They trace the trend from Star Wars' Early Bird empty-box certificate and the Cabbage Patch Kids craze through Nintendo consoles, Tickle Me Elmo, Hatchimals and Fingerlings, and argue that scarcity marketing, holiday-season advertising, media buzz, and fear of missing out drive the frenzy. They cover retailer "hot toy" lists and whether they are paid placements (Amazon, Walmart, Target), the Sears/JCPenney/Montgomery Ward wish books, toy flippers and resellers who use bots, and a tongue-in-cheek guide to reselling toys. They close with their picks for this year's hot toys (Bloom dolls, Hatchimals, L.O.L. Surprise, Lego Make Your Own Movie kit, Fisher-Price Llamals, Playmobil) and a listener mail message from a teacher.
topics: paid placement on retailer hot toy lists

entities.name: Lego Make Your Own Movie kit

segments.title: Seattle tour plug and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh plugs January Seattle show dates at The Moore Theatre and ticket sources. The hosts banter about early Christmas retail, Josh's holiday tweet, and their childhood toys, including a Cabbage Patch Kid.

segments.title: Cabbage Patch Kids and the first must-have Christmas toy
segments.summary: Chuck argues Cabbage Patch Kids created the modern must-have Christmas toy, as Jaws did for the summer blockbuster. Josh disputes this, pointing to earlier hot toys such as the Star Wars Early Bird empty box, Mr. Potato Head, and Robert the Robot. They also discuss the Atari Pac-Man cartridge and the violence around hot toys, and the hosts note that Coleco sent dolls to reporters and that supply fell short of demand.

segments.title: Nintendo, Golden Eye, and Tickle Me Elmo
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Nintendo's dominant Christmas products, Golden Eye on the Nintendo 64, and Tickle Me Elmo, which led to a Walmart employee being trampled. They also mention Hatchimals' popularity from 2016 to 2018.

segments.title: Wish books and the shift in how kids learn about toys
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the Sears, J.C. Penney, and Montgomery Ward catalogs known as wish books, and the Wish Book Web site that scanned them. They compare how kids picked gifts from catalogs with today's online lists.

segments.title: Retailer and third-party hot toy lists
segments.summary: The hosts examine who makes hot toy lists, including third-party sites like The Spruce and Toy Insider and retailers like Amazon, Walmart, and Target. They report that Amazon and Walmart reportedly charge brands for placement, while Target's list does not appear to, and they note that appearing on a list can make a toy a hot seller.

segments.title: Holiday marketing, advertising, and scarcity
segments.summary: The hosts explain how marketers use holiday mood and nostalgia, citing a University of Hertfordshire count of 100 ads in three hours of Saturday morning kids programming. They argue that scarcity marketing, fear of missing out, and the desire to be a 'have' drive must-have toy frenzy. They cite Disney Vault releases, Hatchimals' spin Master's disputed scarcity claims, Fingerlings' production ramp-up, and supermarket limit signs.

segments.title: Toy flippers, bots, and reselling
segments.summary: The hosts condemn toy flippers and ticket scalpers, though Josh is more tolerant of individuals reselling occasionally. They describe how bots buy limited-stock items within seconds and then resell them. They also discuss an Investopedia guide to reselling toys and Michael Larson comparison.

segments.title: This year's must-have toy picks
segments.summary: The hosts say they cross-referenced lists from Target, Toys, Tots, Pets and More, Amazon, the Today Show, Toy Insider, the Spruce, Walmart, and New York Magazine. They highlight Bloom dolls, Hatchimals, Barbie Dream Plane, L.O.L. Surprise, Ryan's World unboxing videos, Lego Make Your Own Movie kit, Fisher-Price Llamals, and Playmobil.

segments.title: Listener mail from a teacher
segments.summary: A teacher named John L. Bushkin writes that his students enjoy the hosts' characters and encourages them to keep sharing strong opinions in episodes.

segments.title: Sign-off and contact information
segments.summary: The hosts invite listeners to get in touch via the website, social links, or the stuff podcast email address, and close the episode.
